verdicts.why: Names a means or a tool without any stance toward it; the sentences show it used as a plain label for the piano.
Names a feeling of trust in plain terms; the speaker takes no side about whether the trust is warranted.
Names a trusting relationship descriptively, with no approval or contempt beyond the meaning.
Names a secret entrusted to someone; a neutral label for the thing confided.
Names the breaking-in event plainly; the packet itself has 'it does not follow that the interruption must be unwelcome', showing the word carries no verdict.
Names the act of breaking continuity without judging the one who breaks it.
Names a pause in time; purely descriptive.
Names an informal entitlement without saying whether it is deserved; 'society has claims on us all' is neutral.
Names the assertion of a right in plain legal terms, neither endorsing nor doubting it.
Names a demand for something as due; the word takes no attitude toward the demander.
The plainest word for taking in food; it is the neutral neighbour that loaded words like 'devour' or 'gobble' are measured against.
Names having a meal with no attitude toward the eater.
Plain word for animals feeding; the restriction to animals is a selectional fact of the sense, not a judgement on anyone.
Names careful looking-over; the apothecary examining a patient or a visitor examining a house carries no stance.
Names detailed analysis descriptively, without approval or contempt for what is analysed.
Names close questioning as a neutral procedure; unlike 'grill' or 'interrogate' it implies nothing about the questioner's hostility.
Plain word for putting on clothes; no attitude.
Plain word for clothing someone; no attitude.
Names the manner of dressing without the word itself judging it; any judgement comes from the adverb ('simply dressed'), not from 'dress'.
Formal, neutral word for acting in accordance with a request; unlike 'submit' or 'knuckle under' it says nothing about the complier's weakness or the rightness of the demand.
Names a painful emotion; the referent is unpleasant but the word describes the feeling without taking a side about the person who feels it.

In 'it will be quite a shame if he does not' the word is the speaker's own sympathetic regret - informal, gentle disappointment, never disgrace or reproach - which a learner who knows only the guilt sense will misread.
Names moral goodness; the approval is the meaning itself, not a colouring laid over a neutral referent.

Moralising and gendered: applied almost only to women, it equates chastity with a person's whole goodness and makes its loss a fall ('a sister's sense of decency and virtue'), a euphemistic frame a learner must not use innocently.
Names a particular good quality ('every virtue'); the approval is the meaning, with no attitude beyond it.
